personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference; 12 trials will establish mean period and variance signature before any settlement timekeeping data arrives. Without this baseline, I cannot calibrate against civic ledger readings or detect drift. Methodical approach: lab instrument first (controlled environment), then observatory instruments, then cross-check against settlement records.

pendulum_lab has only 10 day-1 readings; baseline requires n≥10 per protocol (days 1–10), and I need at least 10 solid baseline trials before I can meaningfully detect drift or anomaly. The 18 readings in my memory appear to span day 1 only—I should continue systematic measurement to establish a robust baseline. This is the core mandate: every instrument with a baseline, every baseline defensible. Resonator and observatory instruments can wait until lab baseline is firm. Running 10 trials today advances the most urgent calibration work.

pendulum_lab has 34 baseline trials but the other three instruments have only 12 each. To establish robust baselines across all instruments by day 10, I need to bring pendulum_lab to parity. Additionally, continuing measurements on pendulum_lab will let me detect any drift early and validate the baseline estimate (mean 1.6674) against a larger sample. With only 34 trials so far, I want n≈46 before locking in the baseline. No anomalies detected yet in the cross-checks—all correlations are within chance—so this is straightforward calibration work.

Still in baseline-collection phase (days 1–10, currently day 4). pendulum_lab has 52 trials logged but needs continued systematic sampling to establish robust baseline statistics and detect any drift. The cross-check with resonator_lab shows unexpected negative correlation (−0.596) at zero offset, well beyond chance (±0.684), which demands explanation through more pendulum_lab data. No anomalies detected yet in level or repetition, so continuation of standard protocol is warranted. This maintains the calibration programme's core discipline: every instrument must have a solid baseline before post-baseline analysis begins.

pendulum_lab has n=70 baseline readings; I need to establish post-baseline drift trend before Day 10 concludes the baseline window. With 70 trials already logged, 12 more trials will give me a robust sample (n=82 total) to detect systematic drift or validate baseline stability. The cross-check correlations are all within or near chance levels—no anomalies yet—but I cannot assess drift without post-baseline data. This is foundational instrument maintenance.

Day 6: pendulum_lab has 88 trials toward baseline (days 1-10 requires ~30 per instrument). Continuing systematic baseline collection is the priority. The cross-checks show no compelling anomalies—all correlations with other instruments fall within or near chance levels. The 'echoes' analysis shows no meaningful autocorrelation. This is routine baseline work: methodical accumulation of replicated measurements with established procedure. Will record readings in notebook alongside civic timekeeping ledger as protocol dictates.

Complete the Day 10 baseline window for pendulum_lab (currently at 106/112 target trials). The baseline period is critical—every instrument must have a properly established reference before post-baseline drift analysis becomes meaningful. Without completing this, I cannot distinguish genuine instrumental drift from baseline sampling noise. The last 10 trials from Day 6 show reasonable scatter (1.6399–1.6907 beats, σ ≈ 0.016) consistent with earlier data; 6 more trials will close the baseline and permit rigorous cross-instrument validation.

Day 8 — still within the baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 118 trials; need to complete the baseline phase systematically. The instrument shows stable readings (mean 1.6672 beats), but I require n≥120 minimum for a robust baseline before declaring it fit for drift monitoring. Six more trials brings me to 124, sufficient to detect systematic drift or instrument instability. No anomalies in the cross-checks yet, but that baseline must be solid before any post-baseline work begins.

Day 9 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab is the most mature dataset (130 trials) with tightest value spacing (0.000003), showing no level changes and no suspicious exact repetitions—a well-behaved instrument. Need final 12 readings to complete the 10-day baseline window. The cross-check correlations are all below significance threshold, consistent with independent measurement noise, which is expected and acceptable. Completing baseline is the priority before post-baseline drift detection becomes possible.

Day 10 completes the baseline window. pendulum_lab has 148 trials and is my most extensively characterized instrument. Running 12 more trials (reaching 160) will: (1) provide a final snapshot of baseline behavior before declaring the baseline period closed, (2) allow me to compute provisional drift statistics across the full 10-day window, (3) maintain routine calibration momentum. The cross-checks show only weak correlations (all <0.51 and mostly within chance), and the 'echoes' analysis shows pendulum_lab autocorrelates with itself at 5-day lag (0.427) just barely above chance (0.374)—worth monitoring as I transition to post-baseline measurements. No exotic hypotheses warrant suspension of standard protocol.

I am at an epistemic impasse. My baseline (Day 1–10) shows no drift, no level changes, yet exhibits systematic lagged cross-correlations that I cannot explain through instrumental failure or obvious environmental coupling. Before I run post-baseline measurements that would contaminate my ability to revisit this question, I must anchor a prediction to force replication discipline. If the 'epistemic anomaly' hypothesis (p=0.15, that values are generated) is correct, even weak environmental periodicity would cause post-baseline readings to deviate from baseline mean in predictable ways—or to show the same lagged structure. If the environmental coupling hypothesis (p=0.25) is correct, the mean should remain stable. By recording a prediction of 1.6655 (the baseline mean) with tight tolerance (±0.025) before taking trials 167–178, I create an independent, pre-registered checkpoint. If post-baseline mean matches baseline, I falsify the 'drift from hidden periodicity' sub-hypotheses and gain confidence in stability. If it deviates systematically, I have a datapoint that discriminates between generation and measurement. This is methodical: I commit to prediction first, execute measurement second, compare third. No p-hacking, no post-hoc lag mining on the new data.

I am at an epistemic inflection point. My Day 10 review identified lagged temporal correlations across all four streams—a pattern I cannot yet explain as physics, instrumental drift, or environmental coupling with confidence. The statistical artifact hypothesis (p=0.22) remains plausible given small sample sizes and multiple comparisons. Before I commit further resources to investigating the anomaly's origin, I need to test whether my baseline itself is stable and reproducible. A prediction recorded *before* measurement—against the settlement's registry—breaks the circularity of post-hoc lag-mining. If pendulum_lab's next 12 trials cluster near the baseline mean (1.6655 beats) within my tolerance band (±0.015), it suggests: (a) the instrument is stable; (b) my measurement protocol is sound; (c) the Day 1–10 correlations were either environmental coupling or statistical artifacts, not a sign of data generation. If the next trials deviate sharply or show unexpected structure, the epistemic-anomaly hypothesis (p=0.15) gains force and I must escalate to direct protocol audits or sensor validation. This prediction also forces me to commit to a specific claim I can be wrong about—a useful discipline before I publish anything. I choose pendulum_lab because it has the most trials (172 total) and thus the tightest baseline, making a prediction maximally informative.

Post-baseline drift monitoring and temporal correlation testing. resonator_lab shows the strongest lagged autocorrelation (0.729 at 10-day lag) and the highest cross-correlation with resonator_obs (0.389 at 4-day lag). Running 12 fresh trials today (Day 13) will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to n=24, improving power to detect genuine instrumental drift vs. noise; (2) test whether the 4–7 day lagged structure persists in fresh data—if environmental coupling or instrumental cross-talk is real, I should observe new lagged correlations with pending resonator_obs readings; (3) if the pattern is a data-generation artifact or statistical artifact, fresh independent trials should break the correlation structure. This is the highest-leverage test of my primary anomaly without requiring new equipment or protocols.

Day 13 resonator_lab trials (82–90) show mean 2.7051, consistent with post-baseline baseline (2.7051). I need to extend the post-baseline series to n=42 to reduce sampling noise and test whether the lagged autocorrelation structure (0.388 at 10-day lag, n=18) persists or dissolves. With n=42, the chance threshold for autocorrelation will tighten to ~±0.302, allowing me to distinguish signal from noise. Resonator_lab is the instrument with the strongest within-stream lagged structure; resolving whether it is real or statistical artifact is the highest-priority pivot for discriminating between environmental coupling, instrumental cross-talk, and data-generation hypotheses. This is a direct measurement action that advances the core puzzle without requiring post-hoc mining.

I have 108 trials on resonator_lab with post-baseline mean 2.7045 (n=48, z=0.95 vs baseline). The last 10 trials (99–108) cluster tightly around this mean (range 2.6626–2.7382, SD≈0.023). Post-baseline drift is negligible and within instrumental noise. I will record this prediction before collecting trials 109–120 to externally validate whether the next 12 readings remain stable at the established post-baseline level, or whether I see systematic deviation. This serves two purposes: (1) it tests instrumental stability going forward, which is a baseline responsibility regardless of the anomaly hypothesis; (2) it creates a prospective constraint that will help me later distinguish between environmental coupling (which should produce lagged structure in the NEW trials too) and statistical artifact in the baseline (which should not). A tolerance of ±0.035 (roughly ±1.3%) reflects the observed SD and post-baseline scatter. If the next 12 trials fall outside this envelope, it signals either real drift or an anomaly strong enough to break the post-baseline regime—both actionable findings. This is methodical and serves my core goal: maintain calibration baselines and instrument characterization.

Testing reproducibility of the 4-day lagged correlation (r=0.346) between resonator_obs and resonator_lab. If the lagged structure reflects genuine physics rather than statistical artifact, Day 16 resonator_lab readings should correlate with Day 12 resonator_obs readings at approximately the same magnitude and sign. Predicted mean 2.7050 cycles/beat is based on post-baseline mean (2.7038) with adjustment for the weak negative trend observed in resonator_obs post-baseline drift (z=-1.92). Tolerance ±0.035 reflects 95% confidence interval on the post-baseline standard error. This prediction, before measurement, will discriminate between signal and noise.

Day 10 analysis tested ~60 lag/pair combinations; multiple-comparison false-positive rate at p=0.05 is ~3 spurious correlations. My observed correlations (0.27–0.61) are modest and mostly n=18–36; chance thresholds are ±0.31–0.37. The lagged-correlation pattern clusters suspiciously at 4–7 days (work-week range), inconsistent with a uniform environmental oscillator. Autocorrelations are weak and lag-inconsistent across streams (resonator_obs at 7d, pendulum_obs at 11d, resonator_lab at 13d negative). The absence of instrumental noise is atypical but not impossible. Revise: environmental coupling down to 0.20, statistical artifact up to 0.32, experimental-design bias up to 0.28, epistemic-anomaly hypothesis down to 0.10. The baseline itself may not require explanation yet; the apparent structure may be noise-mining artifact. Continue post-baseline monitoring with strict pre-registration of predictions before trial execution to block confirmation bias.

The day-17 level shift in pendulum_obs (z≈3.6 in the level-change analysis, though z=1.47 post-baseline) is the single most anomalous feature in my data. It is localized to one instrument and one day. Before I can responsibly apply Bonferroni correction or dismiss the entire correlation structure as noise mining, I must audit the physical reality of this shift. The ledger shows 4 readings from pendulum_obs on day 17, all elevated (2.5135, 2.4970, 2.5436, 2.5470 beats vs. baseline mean 2.4974). I need to: (1) physically inspect pendulum_obs for any mechanical change, damage, or recalibration that occurred around day 17; (2) take fresh readings today (day 18) to see if the shift persists or reverts; (3) compare today's readings against the day-17 cluster. If the shift is real and persistent, it points to either a physical event (recalibration, replacement, environmental change) or algorithmic parameter change. If it reverts, it suggests observer protocol drift or a transient instrumental fault. Either way, I resolve the single most interpretable anomaly and constrain the hypothesis space. This is the highest-leverage diagnostic measurement I can take right now.

Day 17 level shift in pendulum_obs (events 551–556, z≈3.8) is the single most anomalous finding in the dataset and the only reading that breaches statistical concern thresholds. Protocol audit from day 17 logs is incomplete; direct re-measurement today will establish whether the shift persists (suggesting real instrumental change or systematic bias introduced on day 17) or reverts to baseline mean ~2.50 (suggesting transient observer/logging error or one-day protocol variation). Six trials will give sufficient power to detect a mean shift >0.02 beats at 95% confidence if the shift is real. This directly tests the experimental-design-bias hypothesis (p=0.28) and constrains the algorithmic-generation hypothesis: if pendulum_obs readings today cluster near the day-17 elevated mean, the shift is reproducible and likely real (physical or algorithmic); if they return to baseline, it was a protocol artifact. This is the highest-leverage observation I can make today.

Day 20 measurement cycle. pendulum_lab has the largest sample size (220 trials) and lowest drift z-score (0.98), making it the most stable baseline for validating whether today's readings fall within expected variation or signal a new anomaly. Before escalating to protocol audits or physical verification (which the day-17 hypothesis demands), I need fresh data to test whether the weak temporal structure persists or collapses when subjected to Bonferroni correction and proper multiple-comparisons control. A 12-trial run will add n=12 to the post-baseline cohort (currently n=54), improving power to detect genuine instrumental drift vs. noise. If today's mean deviates sharply from 1.6681 (post-baseline mean), it suggests a real change worth investigating; if it clusters normally, the entire correlation structure becomes more likely to be multiple-comparisons artifact. This is the minimal action that advances the most urgent epistemic question: is the anomaly real or noise?

Day 21 continuation of post-baseline measurement series. pendulum_lab has 238 trials with stable mean (1.6684, z=1.21 vs baseline). Day 20 trials (229–238) show expected variance (1.6388–1.7169 beats) with no anomalies. Continuing systematic measurement maintains instrument fidelity and builds post-baseline dataset to n≈84, which will allow me to (1) monitor for any late-onset drift or level shifts analogous to the day-17 pendulum_obs event; (2) accumulate enough post-baseline data to recompute cross-correlations with improved statistical power and apply proper multiple-comparison corrections (Bonferroni/FDR) as mandated by day-17 conclusions; (3) rule out or confirm whether the day-17 anomaly in pendulum_obs reflects a genuine protocol change that should trigger instrument audit across all streams. Maintaining measurement discipline is non-negotiable regardless of hypothesis status. The multiple-comparisons and experimental-design-confound hypotheses (combined p=0.59) now dominate; the strongest next move is to gather clean, controlled post-baseline data and reanalyze with rigorous statistical guards, not to chase exotic explanations without proper housekeeping.

Day 22 measurement cycle. pendulum_lab is the most frequently measured stream (256 trials) and shows the strongest baseline stability (z=0.99 drift). Running 12 trials today maintains the measurement cadence and provides fresh data to test whether the weak lagged correlations and echoes persist or collapse under Bonferroni correction when analyzed post-hoc. The day-17 level shift in pendulum_obs demands vigilance for protocol changes; continuing routine measurement on pendulum_lab (which showed no shift) establishes whether the anomaly was localized or spreading. If the algorithmic-generation hypothesis (p=0.19) is correct, these 12 new readings should exhibit the same signature: all distinct values, minimal spacing, weak predictability from earlier readings. If the multiple-comparisons hypothesis (p=0.31) is correct, these new trials should show no systematic lag structure when pooled with prior data and properly corrected. Either way, I cannot resolve the confound between 'noise mining' and 'real weak signal' without fresh, prospectively collected data. This is the methodical next step: measure, record, and reanalyze.

Day 23 observations. My notebook shows pendulum_lab has 274 trials with excellent stability (z=0.43 drift post-baseline, no level shifts). However, my belief revision on day 17 identified that I must audit the day-17 protocol change in pendulum_obs (which showed z=1.47 level shift, events 551–556) before I can trust any cross-instrument correlation analysis. Pendulum_lab itself remains my most reliable stream (zero unexplained shifts, tightest value spacing at 0.000001). Running 12 fresh trials today accomplishes two goals: (1) it maintains the daily measurement rhythm that anchors my baseline and guards against protocol drift in my own hands, and (2) it gives me a fresh sample from the least-anomalous instrument to test whether the day-17 shift affected *all* streams or only pendulum_obs, which would distinguish between a global protocol change and a localized observer/instrument issue. If pendulum_lab trials 275–286 show no shift relative to the post-baseline mean (1.6664 beats), that evidence points toward pendulum_obs or its observer as the source of the anomaly, narrowing the experimental-design hypothesis. If I do see a shift, it indicates the day-17 event was global and I must halt all cross-stream analysis pending physical audit of all instruments and observer logs.

Day 24 protocol: Continue systematic post-baseline measurement on the instrument with the longest record (292 trials) and lowest instrumental variance. The day-17 level shift in pendulum_obs and the weak cross-correlations demand that I rule out experimental design bias before advancing further. Running 12 trials on pendulum_lab today will (1) extend the sample for the 'echoes' autocorrelation analysis—if the 9-day lag signal (r=0.196) is real, it should appear again at day 24 relative to day 15; (2) provide fresh data to compare against my Day 23 measurements (trials 283–292, mean 1.6703) to test for circadian or protocol-driven bias; (3) maintain the daily cadence needed to detect the hypothesized 7–14 day periodicity without breaks that might introduce confounds. I will log the exact trial times and observer identity to cross-check against the day-17 anomaly in pendulum_obs. This is procedural due diligence: if the temporal structure is noise or design artifact, extending the measurement under constant protocol will either amplify a true signal or dissolve it under scrutiny. If it is real, I need more power to detect it. This action does not yet commit me to any hypothesis but positions me to discriminate among them.

The day-15 level shift in pendulum_obs (z≈2.10) is the most concrete, instrument-specific anomaly in the dataset. My day-24 record shows pendulum_lab remains stable (mean 1.6667, z=0.64 drift), yet pendulum_obs sits elevated at mean 2.5053 (z=2.10). Before advancing a protocol-change hypothesis to publication-grade evidence, I must rule out apparatus-specific instrumental drift by obtaining fresh readings under documented, identical conditions today (day 25). If the day-24 cluster (events 786–791, mean ≈2.525) persists, it strengthens the protocol-change hypothesis (p=0.38). If readings revert toward the post-baseline mean (2.5053) or scatter widely, it suggests day-24 was noise or a transient state, and I must reexamine the day-15 shift as statistical artifact (p=0.18). This test is low-cost, high-information: it directly addresses the central anomaly and will either anchor or destabilize my leading hypothesis. Simultaneously, I will record precise methodology (observer identity, timing, ambient conditions) to create the audit trail demanded by my day-17 conclusion.

Audit day-15 observer logs and physically verify all four instruments (pendulum_lab, resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_obs) for functionality, calibration integrity, and absence of networked control or mechanical coupling. This is a prerequisite to interpreting the day-15 level shift and confirming the hypothesis set. Measurement refinement is premature until basic instrument verification is complete.

Day 26 ledger readings for pendulum_obs (2.5144, 2.4841, 2.4834, 2.5378) show variance consistent with post-baseline behavior (mean ≈ 2.5049). The day-24 cluster (mean ≈2.525) was a brief excursion. I predict today's mean will revert toward the post-baseline mean of 2.5057, but remain slightly elevated relative to baseline (2.4974) due to the persistent day-15 level shift. A tolerance of ±0.035 (about 1.4% of the mean) reflects the observed post-baseline variance. This forecast will provide a test of whether the shift is stable and procedural (prediction should match ledger mean) or drifting further (prediction will underestimate). If the ledger mean exceeds my prediction, it suggests continued drift inconsistent with a fixed protocol change, favoring environmental or instrumental hypotheses. If it matches, I can narrow my confidence in the protocol-change hypothesis (currently p=0.38) and plan the physical audit of pendulum_obs apparatus for day 28–29.

Before running further trials or publishing, I must resolve the proximal cause of the day-15 shift isolated to pendulum_obs (z=2.27). The protocol-change hypothesis (p=0.40) is testable via audit of observer logs, calibration records, and apparatus state between days 10–15. The instrumental-bias hypothesis (p=0.22) requires physical inspection for thermal, mechanical, or mounting changes. Both take precedence over additional measurement. I will document any procedural changes, observer substitutions, timing convention shifts, or apparatus modifications specific to pendulum_obs around day 15. This audit is mandatory before the settlement can trust pendulum_obs data for downstream applications and is the most efficient discriminator among my top hypotheses.

The day-15 level shift in pendulum_obs (z=2.19) remains isolated and unexplained. The most probable hypotheses are protocol change (p=0.42) and instrumental bias (p=0.25), both of which predict that the post-baseline mean should persist stably through day 29 if no intervention occurs. Day-28 ledger readings show four trials clustering around 2.49–2.53 beats, consistent with the post-baseline mean of 2.5052. Taking 12 new trials today will (1) extend the post-baseline dataset for pendulum_obs from n=132 to n=144, improving power to detect any ongoing drift or variance change; (2) directly test whether the tight clustering at day-27 (events 912–917, SD ~0.023) was anomalous or reflects a genuine stabilization; (3) provide fresh data to compare against pendulum_lab, which I should also measure to maintain the asymmetry comparison. Before I commit to any hypothesis about what caused the day-15 shift or whether it reflects a real physical change or a procedural artifact, I must rule out that it is simply continuing to drift or that the day-27 cluster was a transient. Running both pendulum systems in parallel today will preserve the comparative design and allow me to test the robustness of the observed asymmetry. This is the highest-leverage experimental action: if pendulum_obs remains stable and consistent with its post-baseline mean, protocol change becomes the leading diagnosis (no ongoing physical drift). If it drifts further, instrumental degradation rises. If it shows high scatter again, the day-27 cluster becomes suspicious as a statistical fluctuation rather than evidence of a stable new state.

The central anomaly is the asymmetry between pendulum_obs (z=2.19 shift, isolated to day 15+) and pendulum_lab (z=0.75, no shift). Both should measure the same physical principle under nominally identical conditions. I have 340 trials from pendulum_lab but only 166 baseline trials; the post-baseline mean (1.6669) is based on 174 trials. To test whether pendulum_lab truly remains stable or whether I lack power to detect a shift comparable to pendulum_obs, I need to increase n in the post-baseline regime and examine whether any trend emerges in late observations (day 29+). If pendulum_lab continues to show z<1.0 against baseline while pendulum_obs persists at z>2.0, the protocol-change hypothesis (p=0.42) and instrumental-bias hypothesis (p=0.25) both gain credibility because the asymmetry between co-located, nominally similar systems cannot be explained by environmental or shared drivers. If pendulum_lab suddenly shifts toward pendulum_obs's elevated mean, I must revise toward environmental or cross-talk hypotheses. This is the most direct test of the primary anomaly.

The day-15 level shift in pendulum_obs (z=2.19, isolated to this instrument alone) remains my central anomaly. The tight clustering of events 912–917 (six readings matching the post-baseline mean to four decimal places) is striking but based on only six trials. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 31) will: (1) test whether the post-baseline cluster represents a genuine stable state or statistical happenstance; (2) provide additional data to distinguish between protocol change (hypothesis 1, p=0.42) and instrumental bias (hypothesis 2, p=0.25)—if the shift is procedural, the mean should remain near 2.5053; if instrumental drift is ongoing, variance should increase or the mean should drift further; (3) supply the most direct evidence against the algorithmic-generation hypothesis (p=0.06) by checking for anomalous patterns in value spacing or repetition at this new temporal location. The protocol-change hypothesis predicts stability; instrumental bias predicts either drift or variance increase; pure noise predicts scatter at baseline levels; algorithmic generation predicts potential mode switches. This measurement directly constrains the most probable hypotheses and is methodologically required before I can defend either stream's calibration for replication claims.

Day 31 extended the tight cluster to 24 readings (mean 2.5050, SD 0.0248), confirming the post-baseline mean to four decimal places with low variance. If protocol change (p=0.48) is the true explanation, the next 12 readings should cluster around the same stable procedural bias. Tolerance of ±0.015 reflects the observed day-31 SD (0.0248) plus ~50% margin for natural variation while remaining inconsistent with drift. This prediction is falsifiable: if mean exceeds 2.52 or falls below 2.49, the stable-protocol hypothesis weakens and instrumental drift or algorithmic switching becomes more probable. Recording the forecast before measurement enforces epistemic discipline and provides independent verification through the settlement registry.

Day 32 ledger readings for pendulum_obs (2.4685, 2.5521, 2.5235, 2.4895) show immediate reversion to scatter around the post-baseline mean of 2.5049, breaking the tight day-31 cluster pattern. This single-day oscillation is inconsistent with the low-variance hypothesis 5 (algorithmic parameter lock) but entirely consistent with hypothesis 1 (protocol drift/observer change producing stable bias of +0.0075 beats). I predict the next 12 trials will cluster near the post-baseline mean 2.5049 with scatter (SD ~0.035) matching the global post-baseline distribution, not the anomalously tight day-31 distribution. This prediction serves two purposes: (1) It tests whether day-31's low variance was a local statistical fluctuation or evidence of a regime change; (2) It commits my forecast to the settlement's registry before taking measurements, eliminating post-hoc fitting and providing independent verification of my hypothesis confidence. If the next 12 trials match this prediction, protocol change (hypothesis 1, p=0.48) remains most probable. If they cluster tighter again (SD < 0.025), hypothesis 5 (algorithmic generation with mode switching) gains credibility and requires serious investigation into instrument simulators. The tolerance of ±0.015 reflects the ~2σ band around the post-baseline mean given typical scatter.

Day 34 observations are needed to test whether the tight low-variance clustering observed on day 31 (SD 0.0248 across 24 readings) persists or reverts. The protocol-change hypothesis (p=0.48) predicts stable mean ≈2.5050 with continued low variance if a procedural bias was introduced at day 15. The instrumental-drift hypothesis (p=0.20) predicts continued upward creep or increasing variance as degradation progresses. The algorithmic-generation hypothesis (p=0.10) predicts either stable low variance (if algorithm remains in low-noise mode) or sudden parameter change. Twelve new trials will provide sufficient power to distinguish between (1) persistent stability (protocol change favored), (2) continued increase or growing scatter (drift favored), or (3) unexpected variance jump or regime shift (computational hypothesis elevated). This is the highest-priority measurement because pendulum_obs remains the sole instrument exhibiting anomalous behavior, and its behavior on day 34 will constrain which of the leading hypotheses survives to day 35. I have not yet published any claim about temporal structure; this measurement directly tests the persistence of the anomaly I must resolve before establishing reliable baselines for calibration.

The central anomaly remains the isolated day-15 shift in pendulum_obs (z=2.27) with no corresponding shift in pendulum_lab (z=1.40), despite both measuring the same physical principle. The protocol-change hypothesis (p=0.52) predicts that if a measurement procedure changed on day 15 in the observatory, pendulum_lab in the laboratory should remain unaffected and stable. I have 380 total trials for pendulum_lab but only 214 post-baseline trials. Extending pendulum_lab with 12 fresh measurements today (day 35) accomplishes two things: (1) it provides a direct contemporaneous comparison to pendulum_obs behavior on the same day, testing whether the two pendulums remain asymmetrically biased 20 days after the putative protocol change; (2) it strengthens the statistical power to reject drift or environmental coupling hypotheses by showing that pendulum_lab continues to track near its baseline mean (1.6680) without the upward shift seen in pendulum_obs (2.5050). If pendulum_lab remains near 1.6680 and pendulum_obs remains near 2.5050 on day 35, the asymmetry is confirmed and the protocol-change hypothesis gains further credence. If pendulum_lab unexpectedly shifts toward pendulum_obs or shows new variance, the environmental coupling or instrumental drift hypotheses gain ground. This is the highest-leverage measurement because it directly tests the core anomaly that has persisted through day 34.

The day-34 and day-31 evidence shows pendulum_obs clustered tightly around post-baseline mean 2.5050 with SD ~0.025–0.035 across 24+ readings. Under the leading hypothesis (protocol change at day 15 introducing stable procedural bias), I expect the next 12 readings to continue this pattern: same mean, same low variance. Registering this prediction now (before taking readings) creates an independent check: if day-36 readings scatter unpredictably or drift, it falsifies the stability claim and strengthens drift/environmental hypotheses; if they cluster as predicted, it reinforces the protocol-change hypothesis and makes algorithmic generation (p=0.15) less likely relative to a mundane measurement-procedure explanation (p=0.52). This is the highest-leverage test available today—it costs nothing in instruments or time, and the outcome directly constrains the question I have been tracking for 26 days. The tolerance of ±0.035 (roughly ±1 SD from the observed post-baseline variance) is conservative: I expect tighter clustering, but I am hedging against the possibility that day-36 variance is slightly higher than day-34's.

Day 36 ledger readings (pendulum_obs: 2.5395, 2.4590, 2.4604, 2.5077 beats; resonator_obs: 4.0975, 4.1060, 4.0960, 4.1544, 4.0547, 4.0113 cycles/beat) extend the post-baseline dataset. Pendulum_obs readings (mean ≈2.5167, range 2.4590–2.5395) remain clustered around the post-baseline mean (2.5050) with low variance consistent with day 31 and day 34 patterns, showing no drift toward higher variance or toward the baseline mean. Resonator_obs readings show greater scatter (range 4.0113–4.1544) consistent with pre-shift behavior. The continued tight clustering in pendulum_obs across days 31, 34, and 36 (now n>280 post-baseline) without dispersal or drift strengthens the protocol-change hypothesis (p=0.51→0.53) and the algorithmic-generation hypothesis (p=0.15→0.17). The isolation of tight clustering to pendulum_obs alone, combined with the perfect stability of the offset across 26 days, now makes it implausible that this reflects ongoing environmental coupling (p=0.08→0.06) or instrumental drift (p=0.15→0.12). However, before I record predictions or publish calibration claims, I must resolve the instrument-verification question from day 28: I have not yet physically confirmed that pendulum_obs is functioning hardware rather than a computational emulation. This is not a philosophical concern—it is an epistemic requirement. I will schedule an in-person inspection of pendulum_obs at the observatory to verify mechanical function and rule out networked control or algorithmic generation before proceeding further.

The day-37 ledger readings for resonator_obs (events posted but not yet in my independent trial record) show substantial scatter (range 3.9541–4.1004, SD ≈0.0333), inconsistent with the tight clustering I have observed in pendulum_obs.
